lessons.title: Entities as Arrays of Structs
lessons.theory:
In data-oriented C, a game entity is not an object — it is a row in a table. All particles, NPCs, or projectiles live in one array of structs, and every system is a loop that reads/writes that array sequentially.

Why? Cache lines on modern CPUs are 64 bytes, and a tight loop over contiguous memory streams them in and out cheaply. One `malloc` per particle per frame, by contrast, scatters the data across the heap and thrashes the cache.

The rule is simple: store the data compactly, iterate linearly, do the work in batch.

worked_example.title: Updating a hundred particles in place
worked_example.explanation: Updating velocity before position (semi-implicit Euler) is far more stable than the naive order — we will use this again in the calculus unit. The struct is 16 bytes (4 floats), so 4 particles fit in one cache line, and the inner loop touches them in the order the hardware prefers.

practice.q: Why is one large array of structs usually faster than one struct per heap allocation?
choices: The compiler can elide bounds checks
practice.explanation: Contiguous arrays stream through cache lines. Heap-per-object scatters the data and the CPU spends most of its time waiting on memory.

practice.q: You add a new field to Particle. What happens to memory layout?
choices: Each element's stride grows; the array stays sequential
Realloc moves every particle to a new location
The compiler silently removes the field
practice.explanation: Strides grow, the array stays packed. (Realloc is only required if the array no longer fits.)

checkpoint.title: Implement semi-implicit Euler for particles
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void integrate(Particle *ps, int n, float dt)`. Apply gravity (G = 9.8) downward: subtract from vy first, then update x and y with the new vy. The harness checks the results against hand-computed values.
static_hints: Update vy first (semi-implicit Euler), then use the new vy when updating y.
Loop `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)` and operate on ps[i] — a struct pointer 'steps' by sizeof(Particle) each ++.

lessons.title: Function Pointers & Behavior Dispatch
lessons.theory:
When every entity in a type uses the same update code, the compiler unrolls the loop. When entities have different behaviors, the obvious C answer is a `switch` on a tag — and the obvious C *problem* is that the switch runs on every entity, every frame, killing the branch predictor.

The fix is to store the behavior as a function pointer in the struct, and call it through the pointer. The signature is uniform; the dispatch is one indirect call, and identical shapes cluster in the same hot loop.

worked_example.title: Per-bot behavior via function pointer
worked_example.explanation: Forward-declaring `struct Bot` lets the function-pointer typedef mention the type before the full struct is defined. The `if (bots[i].update)` guard lets bots opt out of an update step this frame without crashing.

practice.q: Why might a switch-by-tag be slower than a function pointer for AI behavior?
choices: The switch runs every entity every frame, defeating the branch predictor
The compiler refuses to vectorise switches
practice.explanation: An indirect call still does one branch per entity — but it can cluster when most entities share a behavior.

practice.q: What does `void (*f)(Entity*, float)` declare?
choices: A variable f that holds a pointer to such a function
A function f that takes two args
practice.explanation: The parens around `*f` mean f is a pointer; the rest is the function signature.

checkpoint.title: Implement behavior dispatch
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void update_all(Bot *bots, int n, float dt)`. Call each bot's `update` function pointer with `&bots[i]` and `dt`. Skip bots whose `update` is NULL.
static_hints: Pass `&bots[i]` as the first argument so the callback can mutate the bot.
Guard with `if (bots[i].update)` — calling a NULL function pointer crashes.

lessons.title: Tagged Unions (Variants)
lessons.theory:
Real entities come in kinds: a collider is a circle or a rect, an item is a sword or a potion, a packet is a connection or a disconnect. Storing each kind in a different array is wasteful when most fields are common; storing a `void*` loses type safety.

The C idiom is a *tagged union*: a tag enum tells you which arm of a `union` is active. The union is the size of its largest member (plus padding). The tag costs almost nothing, and lets you write `switch (s.tag) { ... }` to safely read the right arm.

worked_example.title: Shape area with a tagged union
worked_example.explanation: The union overlaps `c` and `r` in memory — only one is live at a time. The tag is the contract. This pattern is the foundation of every event system, message bus, and entity component in the later units.

practice.q: Why is the tag stored alongside the union?
choices: The union doesn't remember which arm is active
The tag lets us use a smaller struct
practice.explanation: Reading the wrong arm is undefined behaviour. The tag is the only thing that tells you which arm is live.

practice.q: What is `sizeof(union { Circle c; Rect r; })` (Circle has 1 float, Rect has 2)?
practice.explanation: Unions overlay their members; the size is the largest plus padding for alignment.

checkpoint.title: Implement shape_area
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `float shape_area(Shape s)`. For SHAPE_CIRCLE use `s.as.c.r` with `3.14159265f` for pi; for SHAPE_RECT use `s.as.r.w * s.as.r.h`.
static_hints: Switch on `s.tag` and return the formula for each case.
Use designated initializers (`.as.c = {2.0f}`) to keep callers readable — and to remind yourself which arm is live.

lessons.title: Arena Allocators
lessons.theory:
Per-frame `malloc`/`free` creates fragmentation, the kind of latency that ruins 60 fps guarantees. An arena is a one-shot block of memory with a bump pointer: allocations are O(1) and bumping forward, and "free" resets the pointer when the frame ends.

The contract is the arena owns the lifetimes, not the callers. Perfect for transient per-frame data and per-frame scratch buffers.

worked_example.title: Bump allocator with 8-byte alignment
worked_example.explanation: Alignment matters because some architectures trap on misaligned loads (and even on x86 it is a perf cliff). 8 bytes is the minimum for `double`; you might choose 16 for SIMD types.

practice.q: When is it safe to call `arena_reset`?
choices: When no allocation from this arena is still needed (e.g. end of frame)
practice.explanation: The arena forgets everything on reset. If a pointer escaped and is still in use, the next allocation may overwrite it.

practice.q: Why align allocations?
choices: Performance and to satisfy alignment requirements of some types
practice.explanation: Some architectures fault on misaligned access; on x86/ARM it is a performance trap for SIMD and doubles.

checkpoint.title: Implement arena_alloc
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void *arena_alloc(Arena *a, size_t bytes)`. Round the current offset up to the next multiple of 8, return NULL if the request would exceed `a->cap`, otherwise return a pointer to the slot and advance the offset.
static_hints: Aligned offset: `size_t aligned = (a->off + 7u) & ~(size_t)7u;`
Out-of-memory: return NULL *without* advancing the offset.

lessons.title: Fixed-Size Strings
lessons.theory:
Heap-allocated strings per entity per frame churn memory. In a data-oriented layout, you embed a fixed buffer directly in the struct: `char name[32]`. The price is discipline: every copy must be bounded, every buffer must be NUL-terminated, and `snprintf` is your friend.

The classic bug: `strncpy(dst, src, 32)` on a 32-byte buffer copies up to 32 bytes and does *not* write a terminator when the source is exactly 32 or longer. Always set `dst[N-1] = '\0'` after.

worked_example.title: Bounded string copy
worked_example.explanation: We stop one byte early to leave room for the terminator. If the source is short, we still write a NUL; if it is long, we truncate and NUL-terminate. No buffer can ever overflow.

practice.q: What can go wrong with `strcpy` into a fixed-size buffer?
choices: Buffer overflow if the source is too long
practice.explanation: `strcpy` trusts the caller. In a fixed-size struct that lives in a 100k-element array, this is a one-line remote code execution.

practice.q: After `strncpy` of a too-long source, what must you do?
practice.explanation: `strncpy` does not NUL-terminate when the source is exactly N or longer. Always set the last byte yourself.

checkpoint.title: Implement fs_copy
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void fs_copy(FixStr *dst, const char *src)`. Copy at most 31 bytes from src, then NUL-terminate at `dst->data[31]`. Handles empty strings, exactly-31 strings, and overlong sources correctly.
static_hints: Stop at 31 characters copied; always write the terminator at index `i` (or at `31`).
Be sure the test for 'overlong' still keeps `data[31] == '\0'`.

lessons.title: Vectors: Add, Subtract, Scale
lessons.theory:
A `vec3` is just three floats. Almost everything in 3D graphics is a vector: positions, directions, velocities, face normals, and even color (where you can usually skip the w).

Vector add composes displacements: walking north for 3 meters and east for 4 meters puts you 3 east and 4 north from where you started. Scaling stretches a vector — a negative scale flips it.

worked_example.title: Wind, then thrust, then a missile launch
worked_example.explanation: Notice compound literal `(vec3){...}` — a clean C99 way to return a struct from a function. Every op is a few multiplies; a million of them per frame is nothing.

practice.explanation: Componentwise add: 1+4=5, 2+(-1)=1, 3+2=5.

practice.q: Geometrically, what does 2 * v represent?
practice.explanation: Scaling stretches a vector. (Scale by 0 produces the zero vector.)

checkpoint.title: Implement vector add/sub/scale
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `vec3_add`, `vec3_sub`, `vec3_scale`.
static_hints: Return compound literals: `(vec3){a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y, a.z + b.z}`.
Scaling a vector by 0 should return the zero vector — verify with `(vec3){0,0,0}`.

lessons.title: Dot Product, Length, Normalize
lessons.theory:
The dot product `a·b = |a||b|cos θ` tells you how aligned two vectors are. If they are perpendicular the result is 0; if parallel in the same direction, it's the product of their magnitudes.

Length is just the square root of the dot of a vector with itself. Normalize divides by length to produce a unit vector. The edge case is the zero vector: its length is 0, and dividing by it is undefined. Pick a policy and document it (we'll return the zero vector for safety).

worked_example.title: Are two NPCs facing each other?
worked_example.explanation: We use the dot product for the squared length — cheaper than `x*x + y*y + z*y` written three times. The 1e-6 guard is the policy: 'return zero if too small to normalize'.

practice.q: What is the dot product of two perpendicular unit vectors?
practice.explanation: cos(90°) = 0, so the dot product is 0.

practice.q: Why does normalizing the zero vector require a guard?
choices: The result would be a unit vector
It is slower without the guard
practice.explanation: Without the guard, `v / 0` is undefined behaviour. Pick a sentinel (here, the zero vector) and document it.

checkpoint.title: Implement dot, length, normalize
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `vec3_dot`, `vec3_length`, `vec3_normalize`. For zero-length input, return 0 (scalar) or the zero vector (vec3).
static_hints: Length is `sqrtf(x*x + y*y + z*z)` (or `sqrtf(dot(v, v))`).
Use a tiny epsilon (1e-6) to avoid normalizing the zero vector.

lessons.title: Cross Product & Normals
lessons.theory:
Given two 3D vectors `a` and `b`, their cross product `a × b` is a third vector perpendicular to both. The magnitude is `|a||b| sin θ` — the area of the parallelogram they span. Direction follows the right-hand rule; swap the operands and the result flips sign.

Why you care: triangle face normals (perpendicular to the surface), camera right vector, and torque all come straight from the cross product.

worked_example.title: Compute a triangle's surface normal
worked_example.explanation: The normal direction depends on the winding order: CCW vertices → normal points 'out' by convention. Lighting looks broken if you get this wrong on back faces.

practice.q: What is x̂ × ŷ in a right-handed coordinate system?
practice.explanation: Right-hand rule: fingers curl from x to y, thumb points to z.

practice.q: What happens if you swap the operands of the cross product?
practice.explanation: Anti-commutative: a × b = -(b × a). Winding order matters for normals.

checkpoint.title: Implement cross product and triangle normal
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `vec3_cross` and `vec3 tri_normal(vec3 a, vec3 b, vec3 c)` that returns the unit normal of triangle (a, b, c) assuming CCW winding.
static_hints: Cross product: `a.y*b.z - a.z*b.y` for x, and the cyclic permutations.
Triangle normal: cross of edges `(b-a)` and `(c-a)`, then normalize.

lessons.title: 4x4 Matrices & Transforms
lessons.theory:
3x3 matrices can't express translation as a linear map, so we lift to 4x4 with a homogeneous w-coordinate. We will use the column-major convention (the one OpenGL uses): translation lives at `m[12]`, `m[13]`, `m[14]` (column 3, rows 0–2), and the upper-left 3x3 is the rotation/scale.

A transform stack is just a product of matrices: `M = T * R * S` means *scale first*, *then rotate*, *then translate* (right-to-left in the column convention). The camera pipeline is the same idea grown to three stages: `M_vp = P * V * M` — model (`M`, local to world), view (`V`, world to camera), projection (`P`, camera to clip space, where perspective happens). Recognize the pattern now: every transform you compose is another matrix multiply, and the order encodes the pipeline. We will only need identity and multiplication for now.

worked_example.title: Compose translation and scale
worked_example.explanation: `r.m[col*4 + row]` is the entry at (row, col) in column-major form. The inner loop is the textbook matrix multiply; it is cache-friendly enough at this size and shows up again when you write a real shader.

practice.q: Why do we need 4 coordinates for affine 3D transforms?
choices: Translation is not a linear map in 3D, so we lift to 4x4
practice.explanation: Translation `(x,y,z) → (x+tx, y+ty, z+tz)` cannot be written as a 3x3 matrix-times-vector. Adding a w-coordinate and fixing w=1 lets us represent it as a 4x4.

practice.q: In `M = T * R * S` (column-major), which is applied to a point first?
practice.explanation: Column-major means the rightmost transform is applied first to the point, then the next, and so on. Order matters.

practice.q: In `M_vp = P * V * M`, what runs first on a vertex?
practice.explanation: Right-to-left: M brings the vertex into world space, V into camera space, then P applies perspective into clip space.

checkpoint.title: Implement mat4_mul
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `mat4_identity` and `mat4_mul` using the column-major convention shown above. The harness checks identity×X = X and T(10,0,0) × S(2) applied to point (1,2,3) yields (12, 4, 6).
static_hints: Identity: set m[0], m[5], m[10], m[15] to 1; everything else to 0.
Mul: `r[col*4 + row] = sum_k a[k*4 + row] * b[col*4 + k]`.

lessons.title: Yaw, Pitch & Camera Forward
lessons.theory:
Spherical-to-Cartesian is the most common conversion in a 3D game: given a yaw (rotation around the world up axis) and a pitch (elevation), produce a unit forward vector.

We will use this exact convention (documented in code): at yaw=0, pitch=0 the camera looks down the -Z axis. Positive yaw rotates left (toward -X), positive pitch tilts up. Pitch is clamped to keep `cos(pitch)` from going to zero.

Formula:
  forward.x = -sin(yaw) * cos(pitch)
  forward.y =  sin(pitch)
  forward.z = -cos(yaw) * cos(pitch)

worked_example.title: Mouse delta into a look direction
worked_example.explanation: The clamp keeps `cos(pitch)` from approaching 0, which would make the forward vector flip wildly as the player tries to look straight up.

practice.q: Why is pitch clamped?
choices: To avoid gimbal-like flip when cos(pitch) → 0
practice.explanation: At pitch=±90°, cos=0 and small mouse motion produces huge direction changes. Clamping to ~±89° is the standard fix.

practice.q: At yaw=0, pitch=0, what is the forward vector in this convention?
practice.explanation: Looking down -Z is the OpenGL/Raylib default. Yaw rotates left (toward -X), pitch tilts up (+Y).

checkpoint.title: Implement forward_from_yaw_pitch
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `vec3 forward_from_yaw_pitch(float yaw, float pitch)` with the formula shown above.
static_hints: forward.x = -sin(yaw) * cos(pitch); forward.y = sin(pitch); forward.z = -cos(yaw) * cos(pitch).
If you see huge numbers, you probably forgot the cos(pitch) factor on the horizontal components.

lessons.title: Quaternions: Rotations Without Gimbal Lock
lessons.theory:
Euler angles (yaw/pitch/roll) are intuitive but have a fatal flaw: **gimbal lock**. When two rotation axes align, one degree of freedom is lost — the camera spins on a single axis and can't reach its target. That's why we clamped pitch in the last lesson; clamping hides the symptom, quaternions remove the cause.

A quaternion is a 4-number package `(w, x, y, z)` where `w = cos(θ/2)` and `(x, y, z) = sin(θ/2) · axis` — an *axis-plus-angle* rotation with no order dependence and no lock. Valid rotation quaternions are unit length (`w² + x² + y² + z² = 1`), and two rotations compose with a single multiplication. Blending rotation A into B is done with **slerp** (spherical linear interpolation), which travels the shortest arc at constant angular speed — why turrets, orbiting cameras, and character turns don't snap. Raylib ships quaternion helpers and raymath uses the same struct for camera orientation and bones.

Slerp's kernel: `q(t) = (A·sin((1-t)θ) + B·sin(tθ)) / sin(θ)` where θ is the angle between A and B. A normalized lerp ('nlerp') is the cheap approximation games use for short arcs.

worked_example.title: Slerp for a turret that turns toward its target
worked_example.explanation: The `dot < 0` branch flips B so the arc is always ≤ 180° (quaternions double-cover: q and -q are the same rotation). The `dot > 0.9995` branch avoids dividing by sin(θ) ≈ 0.

practice.q: What does the (w, x, y, z) of a unit quaternion represent?
choices: An axis-plus-angle rotation: (x,y,z) = sin(θ/2)·axis, w = cos(θ/2)
A scale in w and a direction in xyz
practice.explanation: The axis is scaled by sin(θ/2); w is cos(θ/2). Unit length w²+x²+y²+z² = 1 is required for a pure rotation.

practice.q: Why slerp instead of interpolating Euler angles?
choices: Euler angles suffer gimbal lock and don't move at constant speed
Slerp is faster than any numeric solve
practice.explanation: Interpolating yaw/pitch can swing through gimbal lock and take a non-shortest path. Slerp travels the shortest arc at constant angular velocity.

checkpoint.title: Implement slerp
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `quat quat_slerp(quat a, quat b, float t)`. Normalize both inputs, negate b (and the dot) if the dot product is negative, fall back to a normalized lerp when `dot > 0.9995f`, otherwise blend with `sin((1-t)θ)/sin(θ)` and `sin(tθ)/sin(θ)` weights.
static_hints: Normalize both inputs first; only unit quaternions interpolate as rotations.
If `dot < 0`, negate all four components of b and negate dot — that's how you pick the shorter arc (q and -q are the same rotation).
Kernel: `w1 = sin((1-t)θ)/sin(θ); w2 = sin(tθ)/sin(θ);` then blend each component.

lessons.title: Derivatives as Rates of Change
lessons.theory:
A derivative is a rate of change. Given a position function y(t), the instantaneous velocity is `dy/dt`; numerically, we approximate it with finite differences: `(y[i+1] - y[i]) / dt`.

This comes up constantly: estimating speed from logged positions, reading velocity from mouse motion, computing a derivative of any per-frame scalar. The error is `O(dt)` for forward differences and `O(dt²)` for central differences — but central needs a value on both sides of i, so we use forward at the boundary.

worked_example.title: Velocity from a recorded position log
worked_example.explanation: For perfectly linear data, forward differences are exact. For curved data, the truncation error scales with dt; the rule of thumb is 'small enough that you don't care, large enough that float roundoff doesn't bite.'

practice.q: What is the unit of `(y[i+1] - y[i]) / dt` if y is in meters and t in seconds?
practice.explanation: Differences of y are meters; differences of t are seconds. The ratio is m/s.

practice.q: Why is too-small dt dangerous with float?
choices: Roundoff: subtracting two close numbers loses precision
practice.explanation: Catastrophic cancellation: `a - b` where a ≈ b is mostly noise. With dt=1e-7, the velocity estimate can be 100% off.

checkpoint.title: Implement finite_diff
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void finite_diff(const float *y, int n, float dt, float *out)`. Forward difference for `i < n-1`, one-sided at `i = n-1`.
static_hints: For i in [0, n-1): out[i] = (y[i+1] - y[i]) / dt.
Last entry: use (y[n-1] - y[n-2]) / dt — backward difference.

lessons.title: Integration & Newton's Laws
lessons.theory:
Integration is the inverse of differentiation: accumulate rates of change into a state. Newton's second law in code terms: `a = F / m`, then update velocity and position. The order matters — semi-implicit Euler (velocity first, then position) is *much* more stable than the naive order, and is the default in almost every real-time physics integrator.

This is the same operation we did in the data-oriented unit, just with explicit force handling.

worked_example.title: A free body under one force
worked_example.explanation: Stable across the same time step sizes that would let the naive order gain energy and eventually blow up.

practice.q: What does `a = F / m` tell us?
choices: Force per unit mass is acceleration
practice.explanation: Newton's second law. A heavier body accelerates less for the same force.

practice.q: Why update velocity first (semi-implicit Euler)?
choices: Significantly better energy behavior than the naive order
practice.explanation: The naive order `x += v*dt; v += a*dt` is mathematically equivalent for one step but lets systems gain energy over many steps.

checkpoint.title: Implement body_apply_force
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `body_apply_force`. Update vx/vy first using `F/m * dt`, then update x/y using the new velocity.
static_hints: v += (F / m) * dt first, then x += v * dt.
Zero force should leave the body at rest at its position (vx,vy both zero, x,y unchanged).

lessons.title: Euler vs Verlet vs RK4
lessons.theory:
Three integrators you'll see in the wild:

- **Euler (semi-implicit)**: cheap, decent, can gain energy on stiff systems.
- **Verlet**: position-based; `x_{n+1} = 2 x_n - x_{n-1} + a dt²`. Symplectic, stable, great for spring and orbital systems. Velocity is recovered as `(x_n - x_{n-1}) / dt`.
- **RK4**: four evaluations per step, fourth-order accurate. Best for stiff accuracy; expensive and overkill for gameplay.

Boss 0 asks you to use Verlet precisely because the explicit Euler version leaks energy into a spring system — each orbit's swing radius creeps outward every period until the motion looks nothing like a spring. Watch for it.

worked_example.title: Verlet step for a 1D position
worked_example.explanation: Verlet with a constant acceleration has a *closed form* the harness can check exactly: `x_n = x_0 + a·dt²·n(n+1)/2`. Even though the algorithm is the discrete recurrence, we know the answer.

practice.q: Which integrator to reach for first in a typical game?
choices: Semi-implicit Euler; switch to Verlet when energy leaks
practice.explanation: Euler is dirt cheap and good enough for most gameplay physics. Verlet for springs/orbits where energy stability matters. RK4 only for stiff accuracy.

practice.q: How is velocity extracted from Verlet's positions?
practice.explanation: Verlet doesn't carry velocity explicitly; you approximate it from successive positions.

checkpoint.title: Implement verlet_step
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void verlet_step(float *x, float *x_prev, float acc, float dt)`. Compute `x_new = 2x - x_prev + a*dt²`, then set `x_prev = x` and `x = x_new`.
static_hints: `x_new = 2*x - x_prev + a*dt*dt` — that's the whole algorithm.
After computing x_new, assign x_prev = x (the *old* x), then x = x_new.

lessons.title: Lambert's Cosine Law
lessons.theory:
Diffuse lighting — the dim glow of a matte surface under a light — follows `I = intensity * max(0, n·l)`. The dot product is the cosine of the angle between the surface normal `n` and the direction to the light `l` (both unit vectors). A surface directly facing the light is fully lit; one edge-on is unlit; one facing away is in shadow.

This is the foundation of every realistic lighting model and we'll reuse it heavily in the shaders unit.

worked_example.title: Two surfaces, one light
worked_example.explanation: Clamp negatives to 0 — a surface whose normal points away from the light should not go negative (it just goes black).

practice.q: If the light is directly overhead on a flat ground (n=(0,1,0), l=(0,1,0)), the result is:
practice.explanation: Parallel vectors: dot is 1.

practice.q: If the light is behind the surface (n=(0,1,0), l=(0,-1,0)), the result is:
practice.explanation: Negative dot is clamped to 0 in the diffuse model.

checkpoint.title: Implement lambert
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `float lambert(vec3 n, vec3 l, float intensity)` that returns `intensity * max(0, dot(n, l))`.
static_hints: Compute the dot, clamp negatives to 0, multiply by intensity.
Don't forget the `max(0, ...)` — without it, your surface glows when it shouldn't.

lessons.title: Dynamic Arrays
lessons.theory:
Fixed-size arrays are easy and fast but don't grow. A dynamic array amortizes `O(1)` appends by doubling capacity: when full, allocate 2× and copy. The cost of one reallocation is spread across all the cheap pushes since the last one.

Two things to remember: (1) realloc invalidates old pointers — never cache a `&arr.data[i]` across a push; (2) if you store the array by pointer in many places, give out a *new* pointer to consumers after growth.

worked_example.title: A typed dynamic array of ints
worked_example.explanation: Initial cap of 4 covers small use cases; doubling covers up to 2^N without further realloc until the cap grows large.

practice.q: Why is doubling capacity `O(1)` amortized?
choices: Each push is constant except for the rare doubling, which averages out
practice.explanation: Total copies over N pushes is 1+2+4+...+N/2 < 2N, so amortized O(1).

practice.q: After realloc, what happens to old `&a->data[i]` pointers?
choices: They are invalidated (data may have moved)
They still point to the same memory
practice.explanation: Realloc may move the array. Re-fetch pointers after any push that grew the array.

checkpoint.title: Implement da_push
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `int da_push(IntArr *a, int v)`. Grow by 2× when full (initial cap 4 from NULL), append the value, return 0/-1.
static_hints: If `a->cap == 0`, start at cap 4. Otherwise double.
If `realloc` returns NULL, do *not* overwrite `a->data` — return -1.

lessons.title: Hash Maps (Open Addressing)
lessons.theory:
A hash table maps a key to a value in average O(1). The simplest layout is *open addressing*: an array of slots, each with a key, a value, and a `used` flag. You hash the key, look in the slot at `hash & (cap-1)`, and walk forward until you find the key (hit) or an empty slot (miss).

The catch: deletions need *tombstones* to keep the probe chain intact. And keep the load factor under ~0.7 to keep the walk short.

worked_example.title: Get with linear probing
worked_example.explanation: The harness provides the FNV-1a hash, the Entry layout, and `map_put` to set up test entries. You implement `map_get` only.

practice.q: Why keep load factor under ~0.7?
choices: Probes get exponentially longer as the table fills
practice.explanation: Probing chains grow with load. Past 0.7 the table slows down dramatically; at 1.0 it stops working.

practice.q: Why is deletion tricky in open addressing?
choices: You must mark tombstones to preserve the probe chain
practice.explanation: Removing a slot entirely breaks the chain for keys further down. Tombstones mark the slot as 'previously used' so probing continues correctly.

checkpoint.title: Implement map_get
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `int map_get(const Map *m, const char *key, int *out)` using linear probing. Returns 1 with `*out` set on hit, 0 on miss.
static_hints: Start at `hash_str(key) & (MAP_CAP - 1)` (CAP is a power of 2).
Walk `for (int step = 0; step < MAP_CAP; step++)` so you don't loop forever on a malformed table.

lessons.title: Priority Queues (Binary Heap)
lessons.theory:
A binary heap is a near-complete binary tree stored in an array, with the rule that a parent is always better (smaller, for a min-heap) than its children. Insert is O(log n) via a 'sift up'. Pop-min is O(log n) via 'sift down'. A* pathfinding uses this as its frontier.

For an array index `i`, the parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, and the children are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`.

worked_example.title: Sift up after push
worked_example.explanation: The harness will pop everything after your pushes. If you implemented sift up correctly, the popped priorities come out in ascending order.

practice.q: What is the parent index of element i in a binary heap array?
practice.explanation: Children are 2i+1 and 2i+2; the parent is the inverse.

practice.q: Why use a heap instead of a sorted array for an A* frontier?
choices: Insertion is O(log n) instead of O(n)
Sorted arrays are slower to read
practice.explanation: A* inserts and pops constantly; sorted-array insert is O(n).

checkpoint.title: Implement heap_push
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `void heap_push(MinHeap *h, float prio, int val)`. Place the new element at the end and sift up while it is smaller than its parent.
static_hints: Append at the end, then loop: while i > 0 and prio[i] < prio[(i-1)/2], swap with parent.
Don't forget `h->len++` when you append.

lessons.title: Graphs, BFS & Big-O
lessons.theory:
A grid is a graph. A navmesh is a graph. A scene graph is a graph. Breadth-first search visits nodes in layers, finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, and is your first escape from `O(n²)` pairwise checks.

Stored as *compressed sparse row* (CSR) — two arrays, `offsets[]` and `nbrs[]` — it is the most cache-friendly representation we have for static graphs.

worked_example.title: CSR adjacency and BFS
worked_example.explanation: A queue array is enough — no linked list needed. We mark `seen` early to avoid pushing a node twice.

practice.q: 10,000 entities with pairwise collision checks per frame is roughly 50,000,000 checks. Why bad?
choices: Quadratic in entity count — most games pair this with spatial partitioning
The number is too large to print
practice.explanation: O(n²) is the cost you pay for naive pairwise tests. Spatial partitioning (uniform grid, then octree) brings it down to O(n).

practice.q: BFS finds shortest paths in which kind of graph?
practice.explanation: BFS counts edges, not edge weights. For weighted graphs you need Dijkstra or A*.

checkpoint.title: Implement bfs_dist
checkpoint.instructions: Implement `int bfs_dist(const Graph *g, int start, int target)` returning the hop distance, or -1 if `target` is unreachable. Use a malloc'd visited/queue arrays; free them before returning.
static_hints: Allocate a visited array and a queue. Mark the start, push it, and pop nodes until the queue is empty.
Remember: `g->offsets[u+1] - g->offsets[u]` is the degree; iterate from `g->offsets[u]` to `g->offsets[u+1]`.

lessons.title: Boss 0 — CLI Particle Sim
lessons.theory:
This is the world-0 capstone. The starter simulates 3 balls tethered to the centre of a 100×100 box by Hooke springs (force `F = -k·r` pulls each ball back toward the centre; stiffness per ball `K = {40, 30, 35}`). The integration loop uses explicit Euler: position first, then velocity. Watch the orbits — explicit Euler is not symplectic, so every oscillation slowly pumps energy into the system and each ball's swing radius creeps outward, tick by tick. Your job: replace the Euler body with velocity Verlet (kick–drift–kick) and the rings lock in. Verlet is symplectic; its energy error stays bounded forever.

The output must be deterministic (same input → same output every run). All constants are fixed in the starter; the only free parameter is your integration scheme.

What gets checked:
- exactly 600 lines of `T <tick> <id> <x> <y>`
- every position is finite and inside [0, 100] × [0, 100]
- balls actually move (catches a no-op step)
- each ball's outward turning points (radius maxima) stay within 0.5 of the first — a growing amplitude is the energy-leak tell
- two consecutive runs produce byte-identical stdout (determinism)

The starter has a comment marking the exact lines to replace.

worked_example.title: Velocity Verlet for a Hooke spring (kick–drift–kick)
worked_example.explanation: This is velocity Verlet split into kick–drift–kick: a half-kick, a full drift carrying half a kick's worth of acceleration, then a half-kick using the *averaged* old and new acceleration. The average is what makes the scheme time-reversible and symplectic — energy oscillates but never drifts. Explicit Euler applies the old acceleration at the old position; it has no such symmetry.

practice.q: Why does explicit Euler fail the energy check on this spring sim?
choices: It pumps energy into the oscillator, so the swing radius grows every period
The spring constants are too large
practice.explanation: Explicit Euler is not symplectic: it applies the old acceleration at the old position, the per-step energy error never cancels, and amplitude grows like e^(ω²·dt²·t). Verlet's symmetric averaging of old and new acceleration keeps the error bounded.

practice.q: Why must the output be byte-identical between two runs?
choices: Multiplayer replays, deterministic save states, debuggability
practice.explanation: Determinism is what lets a save file, replay, or netcode match across machines. Random numbers or uninitialized memory break it instantly.

checkpoint.title: Implement velocity Verlet and pass the boss
checkpoint.instructions:
Replace the body of `step` with velocity Verlet (kick–drift–kick): compute the spring acceleration at the current position, drift with a half-kick, recompute the acceleration at the new position, then kick with the average of old and new. Constants and output format are fixed in the starter. After 200 ticks all 600 lines must be valid, every position finite and inside [0, 100]², each ball's amplitude stable (later turning points within 0.5 of the first), and two consecutive runs byte-identical.

The starter's comment marks the exact lines to replace.
static_hints: Velocity Verlet needs the spring acceleration twice: once before the drift, once after. Hooke force: `a = -K[i] * (p - C)`.
Kick–drift–kick: `x += v*dt + 0.5*a_x*dt*dt;` then recompute `a(x_new)`; then `v += 0.5*(a + a_new)*dt`.
Run the binary twice; outputs must match byte-for-byte (no rand, no uninitialised memory).
